newsitem.title: USA: Clinton highlights utility stranded costs, ISO's.
newsitem.headline: Clinton highlights utility stranded costs, ISO's.

text.p: The White House said Monday that in the transition to open power markets, electric utilities should be allowed to recover from customers the costs of assets they were required to build or buy in the regulated market.
The annual "Economic Report of the President" also highlighted the need for regulators to decide how strictly to separate ownership of power generation and transmission.
The report by President Bill Clinton's Council of Economic Advisers offered limited answers on the ownership issue, but provided more guidance on stranded cost recovery.

"Investors in regulated enterprises need to be reasonably confident that the government will not renege on its commitments by arbitrarily denying the investors any opportunity to recover their upfront costs," the report said.
But the White House warned that giving utilities an unconditional guarantee of cost recovery might lead to "wasteful investments".

"To avoid creating this incentive, a presumption in favor of cost recovery should apply only for costs incurred to comply with specific regulatory mandates or before competition became a significant prospect," it said.
The report made clear that the White House saw states holding most of the responsibility for handling the issue.
"Much of the potentially stranded costs, perhaps over 90 percent, fall under State jurisdiction, however, and are being resolved by the various States in different ways," it said.

Calling the separation of ownership and control over power generation and transmission one of the "complex issues" that must be resolved, the report pointed to the concept of independent system operators (ISO's) controlling but not owning the power grid as one way to prevent conflicts of interest between transmission owners and power producers.
Again the report made clear that while the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission had issued guidelines for utilities considering creating ISO's, states would have the final say.
"However, the agency (FERC) has left the development and implementation of ISOs to the utilities and the States," it said.
